Poisson regression stands out as a premier choice for modeling count data, particularly when the data exhibits significant variation or skewness. This study focuses on developing and evaluating an adaptive, time-dependent regression model designed for dynamic Poisson processes. The proposed approach employs a generalization of the time-Poiisson auto-regressive (T-PAR) framework, which incorporates time-varying covariates. We introduce the model's theoretical underpinnings, detailing its structural characteristics and asymptotic behaviors. To facilitate parameter estimation, we define an iterative algorithm based on the Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, complemented by a Gibbs sampler for Bayesian analysis. The effectiveness of the T-PAR method is demonstrated through simulated studies and a real-world application involving daily crime statistics in New York City. Results indicate that the model surpasses existing methods in both predictive accuracy and adaptability to changing covariate effects.

Precise stellar photometry serves as a highly effective technique for quantifying atmospheric aerosols. By monitoring the light curves of bright, well-characterized variable stars—specifically the over 50,000 known classical and anomalous Mira variables—this method enables the reconstruction of vertical aerosol optical depth (VOTD) as a function of altitude. The resulting vertical VOTD profiles offer superior insight into microphysical characteristics compared to traditional measurements, which only provide cumulative values along the line of sight. These vertical profiles are derived by integrating the retrieved VOTDs with a radiative transfer model that incorporates a microphysical approach to estimate single scattering albedo. Although developing these three-dimensional (3D) datasets demands extensive computational resources, the resulting data significantly enhances understanding of global aerosol distribution, evolution, and radiative effects. Currently, the availability of automated photometric systems capable of generating vast quantities of stellar photometric data allows for the construction of comprehensive global three-dimensional (3D) models of atmospheric aerosols.

This study introduces Sturdy and Efficient Configurational Molecular Sampling via **Langevin Dynamics**, a method designed to enhance energy-based generative models for biomolecules. These models, including Artificial Neural Networks, DeepMOS, and others, face challenges in training due to the difficulty of satisfying the exact Boltzmann distribution. While recent approaches like Boltzmann GANs and BOLTZ have attempted to resolve this, they rely on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) steps that are computationally expensive and slow to converge. To overcome these hurdles, we substitute the traditional acceptance-rejection step with a single, efficient update derived from the Euler-Maruyama discretization of the Langevin equation. This modification allows the algorithm to generate near-Boltzmann samples with minimal overhead. We demonstrate that our approach significantly accelerates sampling for proteins and nucleic acids compared to existing techniques, delivering a 10x speedup in specific scenarios. Furthermore, we show that integrating this efficient sampler into Boltzmann GANs and BOLTZ results in faster convergence and superior generative performance.

Automatic image description models are frequently evaluated using large-scale datasets like COCO, which serve dual purposes: training these systems and providing reference annotations for evaluation. Although the COCO description references were initially hand-crafted by non-experts to ensure ease of reading, there is currently no guarantee that automatic generation methods fall short of them. We introduce a curated dataset of over 12,000 descriptions for COCO images, meticulously crafted by experts to ensure high-quality standards. Utilizing this curated set, we conducted an examination of various automatic description techniques used within the COCO framework. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art automatic methods significantly surpass the original non-expert references in specific evaluation contexts. Consequently, we argue that current descriptions used for evaluating image captioning systems may introduce unintended biases and advocate for their revision. To address this, we propose a new evaluation metric for image descriptions that mitigates such biases.

This study presents the system models for SISO-OFDM and SISO-OFDM, serving as the counterparts to the models for SISO-OFDM and TISO-OFDM in our previous work. Together, the four models—covering SISO-OFDM, TISO-OFDM, SISO-OFDM, and TISO-OFDM—enable a unified performance evaluation of wideband OFDM systems for simultaneous information transmission and power reception. In these proposed system models, we derive the optimal RF signal design for maximizing end-user quality of service while ensuring minimum quality constraints for other users, as well as the optimal allocation of resources for maximizing total throughput with power efficiency considerations. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed wideband solution offers substantial energy delivery efficiency compared to narrowband alternatives and achieves superior performance in both data rates and energy efficiency in SISO-OFDM and TISO-OFDM scenarios relative to SISO-OFDM and TISO-OFDM options.

Statistical analyses of high-energy physics (HEP) experiments rely heavily on fitting probability density functions (policies, pds) to combine theoretical predictions with experimental data. While various fitting packages exist, they lack a consistent treatment of uncertainty for systematic effects, which complicates the analysis. To resolve this, we introduce a unified framework that handles both statistical and systematic uncertainties within a single likelihood function. This approach allows for a coherent treatment of all uncertainties, enabling the extraction of parameters with well-defined statistical confidence. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness using a binned histogram example, showing how it produces results consistent with established methods yet with superior clarity regarding uncertainty composition. Additionally, we apply the framework to an unbounded histogram case, revealing new insights into boundary conditions and their impact on final parameter estimates.

This study employs a linearized model to investigate the reaction of a turbulent non-premixed jet flame to acoustic manipulation within an active fire scenario. The foundational framework utilizes a flame-front tracking methodology, where the governing equations for a non-premixed jet are linearized around a canonical steady-state configuration subjected to an upward crossflow. The resulting linearized system is expressed as an integral equation, incorporating a Green's function that accounts for the specific geometry of the jet. This formulation integrates source terms representing velocity and temperature fluctuations induced by acoustic waves, which drive the combustion response. Numerical evaluations of the resulting kernel functions are conducted for an incident plane acoustic wave interacting with a round jet. These simulations reveal that the Green's function is significantly influenced by the acoustic Mach number and the spatial alignment of the forcing mechanism relative to the jet. The findings further demonstrate that the flame's reaction to acoustic forcing is contingent upon the wave's characteristics and the nature of the base flow, with the response being notably non-monotonic as a function of the acoustic wavenumber.

Nonlocal gravity emerges as a classical, theoretically equivalent reformulation of modified gravity when modified gravitational source terms are defined through specific constitutive relationships. In this framework, nonlocal modified gravity functions as a causal theory, inheriting well-posed initial value problems from its linear nonlocal ancestor. The nonlinearity introduced by the constitutive relations serves as the mechanism for incorporating modifications to gravitational dynamics. This paper investigates the independence of nonlocal modified gravity from particular source constitutions, identifying the conditions under which the nonlinearity of source modifications can be relocated to the constitutive relations without creating physical inconsistencies. The study further explores the cosmological implications of nonlocal modified gravity, analyzing how nonlinearity manifests within the energy-momentum tensor and the resulting gravitational dynamics.

The LHC has been conducting ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, involving systems composed of protons, lead, and various other combinations, for over a decade. These experiments have revealed that even when colliding lighter systems—such as proton–nucleus, neutron–nucleus, and proton–proton pairs—there is a notable enhancement in the production of high-mass particles and quark-gluon plasma (QGP) signatures when compared to expectations from binary nucleon–nucleon (A + B → C + X) scaling models. These lighter systems hold significant value for mapping out the initial conditions required to generate QCP signatures, as well as for investigating the onset of collective behavior and partonic saturation. Currently, the LHC is running with a new set of light-system collisions, including oxygen–nucleus, argon–nucleus, and others, to explore the unique characteristics of these events and to refine theoretical models.

The detection of X-ray transients in the Galactic Centre region has been a significant discovery, as it revealed that accreting black holes exist within our galaxy. These events are crucial for understanding compact object physics and the evolutionary paths of X-ray binaries. In the past, the discovery of transient events led to the hypothesis that all neutron star (NS) X-ray binaries in the galaxy were responsible for them. Consequently, systems exhibiting steady X-ray emission were classified as containing black holes. However, recent findings have challenged this assumption, suggesting that some neutron star systems may remain in the galaxy centre despite their low outburst frequencies. This paper argues that the recurrence intervals of these transients are simply too infrequent to explain the detection of neutron star systems in the galaxy centre. We demonstrate that the rate of accretion events in the galaxy centre is heavily influenced by the specific characteristics of the source, and we explore the connection between these events and the mechanisms driving X-ray outbursts.

Bipartite graphs are frequently transformed into non-bipartite structures via vertex splitting, a technique widely utilized in algorithms addressing problems like matching and decomposition. Although the resulting graph exhibits an odd cycle for each divided vertex, these cycles often share structural regularities that can be leveraged to recover the original partition. This paper introduces a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm capable of performing such a partition in $O(m+n)$ time relative to the graph's order, specifically with a cubic dependence on the parameter $k$, representing the number of split vertices. The approach relies on a novel cycle detection mechanism and a topological framework for the resulting subgraphs.

Performance degradation attacks, such as those introduced in this paper, serve as side-channel vulnerabilities that can be leveraged to extract top-secret cryptographic keys from targeted systems. These attacks rely on the fact that physical noise generated by software-based performance limiters can mimic the effects of hardware-based throttling. Specifically, the Degreaser algorithm, developed in this work, emulates remote physical constraints by subjecting a server to artificially induced CPU slowdowns. By utilizing only publicly available information about a target, attackers can apply Degreaser to construct a virtual performance cap, effectively replicating the behavior of traditional attacks like Foiled or VarDHL without requiring direct physical interaction or prior knowledge of specific hardware limits. Once established, this software-enforced constraint is used to gather side-channel data through a remote channel, which is subsequently analyzed locally to recover sensitive secrets. The combination of Degreaser with existing methodologies like Foiled and VarDHL has been tested against various server configurations to evaluate their effectiveness under these new attack conditions.

This study examines the strategic regulation of a linearly coupled system comprising $N$ tasks, where the objective is to achieve synchronization among the tasks for a specific duration. The model assumes that the controller possesses full information regarding the collective state of the $N$ tasks but lacks direct access to individual task states. Communication between the controller and the network occurs exclusively through a vector channel constrained by a bandwidth limit. The analysis reveals that synchronization is achievable if the coupling strength surpasses a critical threshold determined by the bandwidth constraint. Furthermore, the study explores the asymptotic behavior of the optimal linear controller as $N$ increases, demonstrating that the optimal strategy simplifies to a weighted average of task integrators in the limit. This limiting policy is shown to be nearly optimal for finite values of $N$ when the bandwidth is sufficiently high. The research offers significant insights into the synchronization of large-scale systems under information constraints, with potential relevance to applications such as multi-robot task collaboration.

This article investigates the representation of regular embedding for the group of rational numbers under component-wise operations within a specific finite variation of a finite structure. By utilizing a Cartesian decomposition technique, the authors establish a structural theorem demonstrating that an almost regular embedding of a product of simple non-abelian groups into a target finite additive variation of a constrained infinite domain occurs exclusively when each component satisfies individually defined regularity constraints relative to the codomain's transformation rules.

Enhancing the high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is crucial for detecting compact-binary inspirals and improving parameter estimation for black-hole mass and spin measurements. Currently, quantum-noise-limited sensitivity in major detectors like LIGO, Virgo, and Kagra rolls off at approximately 300 to 400 Hz due to photon radiation reaction, which acts as an effective damping force on the test masses and mimics classical damping. To surpass this limit, the optical cavity extending beyond the main interferometric cavity must be lengthened; however, increasing this "PuR" (Power Recycling Cavity) to over 10 kilometers is technically challenging. We propose a Sagnac-based optical configuration termed "SloSH" (Sagnac-based Sloher Cavity), designed to mitigate radiation-reaction-induced noise while maintaining a short primary arm and compact external cavities. Functioning as an massive optical resonator, the SLOSH mode offers effective damping reduction comparable to that of extended linear cavities but within a more manageable physical footprint. Complementing this proposal, we also examine a sloshed-Sagnac (SLOSH) design featuring an additional arm to function as an all-one-signal (AOS) detector, potentially eliminating the need for squeezed vacuum inputs to counteract shot noise limitations.

Although deep learning has largely superseded classical approaches, the study of the $N$-gram language model remains relevant. This paper introduces a new method for training $N$-grams using neural networks, which our method termed "Neural $N$-grams" (NN). The core concept involves representing the probability mass function of the $N$-gram as a residual function, allowing a neural network to fit deviations from an initial, fixed prior. This mirrors strategies prevalent in the early days of deep learning. We evaluate various configurations of the proposed NN architecture, training them on the English corpus using both standard and recent, cutting-edge $N$-gram implementations. The results indicate that the neural $N$-grams consistently outperform the base prior and rival other top-tier language models. Furthermore, when combined with established, cutting-edge implementations of $N$-grams, the neural component achieves state-of-the-art performance across several benchmarks, including spurious predictions, zero-shot, and few-shot tasks.

This study introduces the iOCR framework, an intelligent system designed for identifying and categorizing optical character recognition (OCR) errors specifically encountered during the tallying of election ballots. The framework operates sequentially: first, it predicts the most probable error category for a given distortion, and subsequently, a neural network corrects the text based on that specific class. Evaluations conducted on two distinct English-language election ballot datasets demonstrated that this specialized approach significantly outperforms generic, standalone OCR methods. Notably, when compared to leading industry-standard tools, the framework reduced the rate of uncorrected ballots containing at least one undetected error from 11.1% to just 1.4%.

This study examines the circulation patterns of Earth's atmosphere simulated within a global model featuring reduced gravity, employing a anisotropic resolution scheme that offers finer detail in the northern hemisphere. Utilizing a simplified radiative-convective climate scheme, the research explores how circulation dynamics shift as a function of topographic complexity and the presence of an active moon. The analysis reveals that in the absence of mountains and lunar influence, the system develops a zonally symmetric equatorial jet characterized by super-rotational speeds. Introducing realistic topography or a large moon disrupts this symmetry, triggering turbulent baroclinic eddies in the wake of the equatorial jet. These eddies facilitate substantial poleward mass and heat transport, which in turn fosters the formation of mid-latitude jets and zonal winds that oppose the primary equatorial flow. The paper further investigates the transition from cyclostrophic super-rotation to geostrophic turbulence, demonstrating that the resulting turbulent regime exhibits a distinct dependence on the Coriolis parameter. This relationship aligns with theoretical predictions for isotropic high-resolution models and is consistent with observations of the actual atmosphere. Finally, the research indicates that both topography and a large moon enhance atmospheric variability and increase the likelihood of extreme weather events.

This study derives new regularized integral representations for the inverted Gamma function, which are established by extending a recently discovered result regarding the standard integral representation of $\Gamma(z)$ to the context of regularized integrals. These newly developed representations for $\Gamma(1-s)$ are subsequently employed to investigate the relationship between them. Furthermore, a series expansion for the inverted gamma function is derived from these regularized integral forms.

Hydrodynamic theories provide a low-energy effective description of many-body systems, bridging the gap between microscopic models and phenomenological approaches by incorporating internal degrees of freedom such as fluctuations and higher-order correlations. This study introduces a systematic framework for generating hydrodynamic equations via a quantum version of the Müntz closure within the Bose gas context, developed entirely through phase-space Wigner functions. These resulting equations of motion are derived without explicit reliance on the assumption of small density fluctuations, distinguishing them from traditional approaches. Instead, the method relies on expanding the internal variables—representing density and momentum currents—as a series in rank-2 and higher correlation tensors. The validity and performance of these equations are assessed via numerical simulations of a one-dimensional trapped ultra-cold Bose gas containing $10^4$ atoms, featuring both linear and nonlinear interactions under varying thermal conditions. The findings demonstrate that the proposed equations perform robustly across a wide spectrum of temperatures and interaction strengths, significantly outperforming standard hydrodynamic models which lack correlation-based variables.

This study introduces the Instructor-Student architecture, a novel framework designed for knowledge learning. Within this model, the knowledge module is situated between an initial encoder and a subsequent decoder, mirroring the structure of standard Encoder-Decoder models. Specifically, the architecture functions as follows: the first encoder processes the source text to generate an initial representation; this representation is fed into the knowledge module alongside target text, which is then processed by the decoder to produce an output. Distinct from the Encoder-Decoder approach, the output generated from the target text is subsequently re-inputted into the knowledge module to create an enhanced representation of the initial source text.

This article introduces a new compact representation for graphical models, designed to significantly accelerate both constrained optimization for Maximum Entropy and unconstrained Maximum Entropic Path estimation. Our approach defines a set of constraints derived from the graphical model's function, which is then maximized under those limits using Lagrangian techniques. We demonstrate that the resulting solution adheres to specific local consistency conditions, allowing us to define an equivalent function based solely on these consistent variables. Although the resulting function is not strictly monotonic with respect to the original variables, we provide a set of additional constraints to ensure the optimization remains valid. Empirical results indicate that our method achieves a tenfold increase in speed for constrained optimization compared to standard solvers like CBC, and also surpasses existing methods when applied to unconstrained maximum entropy consistency-based models.

Statistical significance testing is a crucial step in the development of high-quality search engines, particularly for evaluating new ranking algorithms. These tests ensure that performance improvements over existing methods are genuine and not merely coincidental. Although various significance tests exist for information retrieval evaluation, most are unsuitable for modern large-scale collections due to computational intensity or reliance on small-sample approximations that lack precision. To resolve this, the authors introduce ExactPPC, a novel algorithm designed for paired permutation tests applicable to any retriever structure. The method delivers an exact solution for the significance of paired comparisons between two retrievers using a specific statistic: the weighted pointwise measure (wP@), which combines precision at $k$ with recall at $N$. The algorithm operates by decomposing the target test into several sub-tests involving simpler statistics, applying exact calculation techniques to these components, and finally recombining the results to yield the final significance value for wP@k. The paper demonstrates that the method remains computationally viable even for massive datasets, requiring only a few seconds to process a 280 GB collection.

Using a multiphase transport (AMPT) model, we examined the elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular ($v_3$) flow components generated in Au+Au and Cu+Cu nuclear collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. These results were compared against the cumulative harmonic analysis (CWA) and the event-by-event (EBE) methods as measured by the PHENIX collaboration. The $v_n$ values were derived from ultra-peripheral reactions via Lévy stable distributions. Our analysis indicated that both the AMPT and Lévy stable models significantly outperform the CWA approach when simulating $v_3$ flows within the multiphase transport (AMPT) framework. Additionally, the findings revealed a strong correlation between $v_3$ and initial geometric anisotropies, as well as a distinct dependence on multiplicity.

Multiphilletracked target filtering is a cutting-edge technique for simultaneously tracking an unknown number of targets with diverse initial counts and varying states, offering strong adaptability and near-optimal performance. However, its mathematically rigorous derivation is often too intricate for practical use. To bridge the gap between optimality and implementability, this study introduces a filter grounded in a hybrid spatial model: one that combines full grid coverage for the birth intensity function with exact modeling only at detected return locations elsewhere. We formally establish the filter's recursive updates under this intensity-based grid framework and demonstrate through numerical simulations that the proposed method closely mirrors the optimal PMBM filter while significantly outperforming conventional intensity approximations.

Soccer represents a highly intricate strategic game where tactical decisions made during critical moments can significantly sway the final outcome. This research investigates the timing and nature of actions taken during these pivotal situations, specifically focusing on the final third of the field. We first introduce a novel deep reinforcement learning framework designed to generate superior play choices in these high-stakes scenarios. Additionally, a new reward structure is proposed to more effectively capture the strategic value of various decisions within the game. Empirical results demonstrate that our advanced actions in the last third of the pitch lead to a measurable increase in winning probabilities compared to standard approaches.

Driven by the growing demand for remote inspection of hazardous or inaccessible structures, such as dams, bridges, and tunnels, there is a critical need for non-contact techniques capable of acquiring structural health data from a distance. This study presents a single-point Laser Doppler Vibrometry (SP-LDV) configuration adapted for two-dimensional (2D) surface displacement mapping. Although effective in close proximity, the direct extension of this approach over large areas is constrained by the limited field of view of the LDV sensor. To resolve this, the authors leverage the principle of virtual imaging, combining SP-LDV with a telephoto optical assembly. By integrating a specific phase-shifting algorithm with a refined 2D reconstruction technique, the system achieves remote surface displacement analysis. Validated through experiments on a cantilever beam, the demonstrated setup successfully retrieves both in-plane and out-of-plane displacements from a range of 1.5 meters, delivering an uncertainty of 0.003 µm for in-plane and 0.012 µm for out-of-plane components within a measured 20 mm virtual image.

This study investigates whether contextualized language models can identify semantic changes in text without requiring specific training for the task. We examine two primary strategies: one involves fine-tuning a contextualized representation using a standard sequence-to-sequence architecture on datasets modified to include alterations, while the other employs a zero-shot approach where a pre-trained classifier predicts changes based on outputs from a contextualized language model. We analyze various types of modifications, including lexical substitutions, syntactic rearrangements, factual corrections, and domain shifts. Our findings indicate that contextualized language models fail to provide a solution for semantic alteration detection. We attribute this shortcoming to the fact that pre-trained contextualized representations do not effectively capture semantic variation, a conclusion supported by additional experiments. Consequently, we advise against using these models for this specific purpose and suggest that future research explore other options.

The masses and spin quantities of galaxies and other celestial bodies hold vital information regarding the intrinsic properties of the universe and the specific characteristics of various astronomical entities. In this study, we utilize the measured masses and rotational velocities of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) within active galactic nuclei (AGN) to establish upper limits for the masses of ultralight (UL) scalar and axial-vector spin fields. Our methodology relies on identifying UL particles through the superradiance mechanism, which amplifies the angular velocities of SMBHs via the accretion of ultralight scalar and axial-vector spins. By integrating theoretical models of UL particle physics with astrophysical observations of AGN, we derive constrained mass ranges for these ultralight particles. Specifically, based on the estimated masses and angular velocities of well-characterized SMBHs, we find that UL scalar particles with masses between $10^{-13}$ and $10^{-20}$ eV face constraints, while UL axial-vector particles are limited within $10^{-19}$ to $10^{-28}$ eV. These findings indicate that UL scalar particles align most closely with the axion model at approximately $10^{-14}$ eV, and UL axial-vector particles match the $\mu$-mesic model near $10^{-20}$ eV.

We examine the final value problem for a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to a time-dependent external force, employing a classical Monte Carlo approach based on the Metropolis algorithm. By representing the solution of the Feynman path integral as a sum over paths, we utilize a Metropolis weight function to construct an efficient sampling strategy. This function is specifically engineered to maximize the information content of the numerical estimate while adhering to computational efficiency constraints. Our simulation results for the solution of the quantum problem align closely with the exact analytical solution derived via the stationary phase approximation.

This paper introduces a novel relational framework for reasoning about quantum programs, incorporating expectations to facilitate the verification of program correctness. Building upon the relational semantics established by Ying in 2016, our relational pre- and postconditions adhere to a binary format, contrasting with the unarity used in standard quantum Hoare logic. Consequently, relational assertions serve a dual purpose: they encapsulate pre- and postconditions within a single predicate and model the transformation of an initial expectation into a final one. We formally define relational quantum logic, deriving key theorems such as logical, conjunctive, and implication rules, along with a relational variant of the Expectation Rule. Furthermore, we develop a relational adaptation of Dijkstra's invariant system for while loops and present a relational correctness definition applicable to quantum while programs. The framework's viability is demonstrated through a mechanized proof of a correctness lemma for Grover's search algorithm, formalized within the Coq theorem prover.

The reliable reconstruction of vector magnetic field components from linear polarization measurements relies heavily on the accuracy of $I$-$Q$ input data. Although $I$-$Q$ data is acquired directly via polarimeters, it is susceptible to biases introduced during image reconstruction and subsequent data processing. These biases are problematic because the target inversion algorithms for atmospheric models assume that $I$-$Q$ inputs are free of such distortions. Interestingly, dust growth does not necessarily suppress the instability; rather, it shifts the most unstable wavenumbers to larger values. These larger wavenumbers correspond to regions with reduced orbital shear, where the orbital timescales are shorter, allowing the instability to persist more effectively. Ultimately, our results indicate that dust evolution reshapes the vertical structure of VSI-driven turbulence, potentially impacting the efficiency of angular momentum transport in the disk's outer zones.

We establish a strong classification result: we prove that any Liouville theorem applies to the bundle of harmonic maps originating from $\mathbb{R}^n$ with target a Liouville Ricci shrinker, provided the shrinking scalar curvature satisfies a uniform bound across the manifold. Utilizing this Liouville theorem as a key tool, we subsequently demonstrate the existence of complete Liouville Ricci shrinkers that possess a non-contracting harmonic bundle.

Neural architecture backdoors represent a form of manipulation introduced during the development of deep learning models, enabling an adversary to embed covert behaviors triggered by specific inputs known as triggers. Once activated, these inputs cause the model to produce outputs that favor a target class designated by the attacker. Although backdoors have been extensively studied in the context of classification networks with fully connected final layers, the phenomenon remains underexplored within architectures employing global average pooling (GAP) to handle feature map downsizing before the final fully connected stage. This paper introduces a new class of backdoors termed "dynamic," which are activated not by visible pixel alterations but by subtle modifications in input preprocessing. Specifically, the trigger manifests as an unconventional resizing technique applied to the image prior to GAP processing. We provide a theoretical framework for these dynamic triggers, detailing their construction and the conditions required for their effectiveness. Additionally, we present a detection strategy designed to uncover these triggers by identifying the anomalous resizing operations. Experiments demonstrate that our dynamic backdoors achieve higher effectiveness compared to traditional triggers and that our detection method successfully identifies them.

The rapid advancement of machine learning, particularly deep learning, has been largely driven by the availability of massive datasets. However, collecting and sharing such extensive data often raises significant privacy concerns and creates practical difficulties. To mitigate these issues, Federated Learning (FL) was introduced, enabling a collaborative training process where a global model is learned across distributed local datasets without the need to physically exchange raw data. Despite its promise, FL faces challenges stemming from non-independent and non-identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) local data, which frequently results in biased global models and unstable convergence.

Addressing the fact that traditional FL algorithms struggle to adapt effectively to data heterogeneity, this paper proposes Stroll, a novel random walk-based framework designed for federated learning. In Stroll, a global model is initialized at a randomly selected participant and iteratively moves between users via a random walk mechanism. This approach allows the global model to be trained exclusively on local data that it has direct access to during its visit. Crucially, Stroll eliminates the requirement for global model averaging at the central server and removes the need to upload global model updates back to the initiator. Theoretical analyses demonstrate that Stroll achieves nearly identical global convergence rates to standard FL methods when data is relatively homogeneous. Furthermore, both theoretical findings and empirical results indicate that when data is highly heterogeneous, Stroll produces superior global convergence compared to conventional approaches.

Although deep learning models excel at supervised tasks, their application in the medical domain is hindered by the scarcity of labeled data. Supervised frameworks are thus often unsuitable for medical image analysis, where segmenting images to identify specific anatomical structures or abnormalities is critical for clinical decision-making. To address this, we explore semi-supervised learning, which leverages both labeled and unlabeled data. Consistent with general image analysis, we posit that unlabeled images from the medical domain share similar distributional characteristics with labeled ones. We therefore develop a novel segmentation framework utilizing a consistency regularization approach, enabling the network to extract features from unlabeled images via an auxiliary classifier trained exclusively on labeled data. Our method integrates a cross-entropy loss function for labeled datasets and combines cross-entropy with Kullback-Leibler divergence for unlabeled sets. We further introduce a simple yet effective data augmentation technique to enhance feature extraction from unlabeled data. Experiments on public medical datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms existing methods.

Single-particle entanglement, or more precisely, entanglement involving single-particle states, is a fundamental prerequisite for various forms of quantum nonlocality and steering. Although these phenomena may initially appear counterintuitive, they are logically consistent and can be realized experimentally using well-established techniques. In this paper, we demonstrate that single-particle entanglement also serves as a necessary condition for single-particle steering, which represents a strictly stronger manifestation of quantum nonlocality that surpasss both Bell nonlocality and EPR steering.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence into the Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) significantly enhances service delivery and operational efficiency within the smart transportation sector. However, the dispersed nature of data in the IoVs creates obstacles for centralized learning models due to storage limitations, privacy concerns, and privacy-related hesitations among users. To overcome these hurdles, the Federated Learning (FL) framework has emerged as a promising solution, enabling a decentralized learning approach that preserves data privacy. Conversely, FL faces its own vulnerabilities, particularly regarding data poisoning attacks and backdoor manipulations. To bolster security and ensure reliable learning, Blockchain technology offers robust solutions through its inherent characteristics of immutability, transparency, and trustless consensus. This paper presents a comprehensive survey examining Blockchain-Enhanced Federated Learning (BEFL) frameworks designed specifically for IoVs. Furthermore, the authors explore key attributes of Blockchain and FL technologies, identify prevalent attack vectors, and categorize BEFL methodologies into four primary models: Naive, Utility-Driven, Attribute-Based, and Protocol-Driven. Finally, the survey outlines the architectural design of these models, detailing their respective learning processes, and assesses their practical viability through simulation studies.

Long short-term memory (LSTMs) are extensively utilized for sequence analysis tasks, such as video identification, yet their substantial computational requirements and memory consumption frequently hinder real-time deployment. This study introduces an algorithm and architecture co-design framework dedicated to optimizing LSTMs for video recognition. The proposed approach combines a novel activation function with a Tucker decomposition method to achieve a compressed representation of the LSTM weights, thereby reducing both the model's size and its associated energy usage. Our designed architecture delivers a multiplicative speedup of 1.7x to 2.1x in real-time processing compared to standard video identification models, while simultaneously achieving a 1.4x reduction in energy consumption.

> We begin by offering a new proof of the Carmichael-Richert theorem, which provides the precise structure of the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_p(X)$ evaluated at $\Phi_n(p)$ for an integer $n \geq 2$. Specifically, $\Phi_p(\Phi_n(x))$ factors into the product of $\Phi_d(x)$ for all $d$ in the set $\{p^k : k \geq 0\} \cup \{n p^k : k \geq 1\}$. Building upon this result, we establish that for any composite integer $N$, the polynomial $\Phi_N(\Phi_n(x))$ is irreducible over the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ if and only if $N$ is not of the form $p^k$ where $p$ is a prime and $k \geq 1$. Furthermore, we investigate the factorization of $\Phi_{f \circ g}(p)$ into cyclotomic terms $\Phi_d(p)$, where $f = g \circ h$ and $h$ is not itself a composition iterate. Finally, we examine the factorization of iterates of the function $\Phi_{f \circ g}(p)$, yielding explicit expressions for the resulting degrees.

We examine the global dynamics of solutions to the initial value problem for the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation with nonlinearities driven by the global spectrum of a Laplacian defined on the initial data domain, which is subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. Specifically, we demonstrate that strong global well-posedness and energy-conserving blow-up solutions can be constructed in the context of the equation in the domain of interest, characterized by the initial data lying within a threshold region of the energy space, defined by a critical regularity threshold. Furthermore, we establish conservation laws for these solutions over infinite time intervals. These findings are instrumental in deriving sharp sufficient conditions for both mass-constrained blow-up phenomena and global existence, applicable to the nonlinear term governed by a supercritical power law in the hierarchy of regularity.

This article serves as the characteristic-zero counterpart to a result by the first author, which was published in the Comptes Rendus Mathematique. That earlier paper established the existence of a semi-parametric, local, uniform, and reduction function for varieties defined within the context of the polynomial ring over the algebra under consideration. These functions ensure that the singular solutions of the problem are resolved in a way that is compatible with specializations. In the present work, these functions are upgraded to be hierarchical and satisfy a stronger form of functionality known as being "subscheme" functional.

Hypathetic tests like Bayes factors (BF) are valuable tools for decision-making in statistical analysis, yet their application has been hindered by a lack of accessible, user-friendly software. This paper introduces a R package designed to facilitate the computation of Bayes factors using diverse statistical models and prior distributions. The code is available at https://github.com/klutch73/bfworkflow. We evaluate the workflow's efficacy through an extensive study of published analyses, demonstrating how the bfworkflow enhances reproducibility and transparency. Additionally, we explore the utility of hierarchical modeling and decision-theoretic approaches within the framework of Bayesian A/B testing for normal distributions. Finally, we present a novel heuristic test aimed at increasing the robustness of Bayes factor calculations.

Discourse markers, also known as pragmatic connectives, are pivotal in signifying the logical connections between distinct textual segments. Their identification and categorization are crucial for a wide array of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, including sentiment analysis, machine learning, and automatic summarization. Building upon the successful precedent of the SenseOverView framework for lexical semantics, this study introduces the DiscSense framework, designed specifically for the automatic classification of discourse markers into semantic categories. The DiscSense process unfolds in four stages: first, a corpus is compiled and annotated to establish a preliminary set of semantic classes; second, these initial categories are refined and expanded; third, the discourse markers are automatically identified and assigned to the defined classes; and finally, the resulting taxonomy is validated. Ultimately, the resulting classification scheme aims to bolster discourse-awareness within various discourse-informed applications. The finalized semantic taxonomy, along with all associated resources and code, is publicly accessible at this link: https://www.aclweb.org/faq/sensebank.

This article provides a concise definition of the Jordanian twist, a specific instance of a Drinfeld twist associated with Jordanian $r$-matrices. The authors demonstrate that the universal $R$-matrix remains invariant under the Jordanian twist and establish the existence of the inverse twist. Furthermore, they verify that the F-matrix commutes with the Jordanian twist and derive the fundamental equation satisfied by the resulting braided vector space. Finally, the paper explores the coproduct of the twisted Lie algebra generated by the universal $R$-matrix.

The goal of this research is to add unconstrained symbolic solving for the language defined by regular expressions extended with intersection and complementation operations. These enhancements to basic union-only regex facilitate the representation of properties for constrained user inputs in system security protocols, such as those found in log analysis tools or access control mechanisms. Furthermore, the developed constraints can be utilized to refine search processes within bug tracking frameworks like Fuzzing and Constrained Testing. Consequently, we introduce a formal framework for representing these extended regex constraints, along with a decision procedure designed to determine their satisfiability. This procedure relies on a novel transformation into a constrained nondeterministic finite automaton (CNFRA), which subsequently undergoes the removal of complementation constraints to produce a deterministic finite automaton with regular constraints (DRFRA). The resulting structure is then subjected to a decision algorithm based on game theory. We have validated the effectiveness of our approach through integration with the Z3 solver within the context of log analysis for security system inputs.

We provide a systematic derivation of the closed-form expression for OPE blocks constructed from two identical primary operators in spinning OPE blocks within the symmetric tensor product space $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta,\ell}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\Delta,\ell}$, where $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta,\ell}$ represents the Hilbert space containing a primary operator of conformal dimension $\Delta$ and spin $\ell$. These operators, defined in the product space, are introduced as a tool for evaluating two-point correlation functions of primaries in the presence of a conformal vacuum two-point function in the AdS$_2$ boundary of AdS$_3$. Furthermore, OPE blocks are recognized as the image of primaries when mapped into the Poincaré disk via an AdS$_3$ isometry, a property that allows us to reconstruct AdS$_2$ correlations by first computing them on Poincaré patches and subsequently integrating over an AdS$_3$ geodesic.

The Multiplexed Lobster-EYE (MuLE) telescope represents a groundbreaking concept designed for extensive X-ray surveying across the sky. This instrument merges the unique Lobster-EYE reflective principle with multiplexing strategies to simultaneously capture images from numerous distinct fields of view. In this framework, a "meta-aperture" composed of hexagonally arranged micro-segments, functioning as the source of "reflections," directs X-rays toward a focal plane where an array of conventional Wolter-type telescopes provides high-resolution imaging for each reflected beam. These traditional sub-units operate as "spiders," tasked with gathering photons and reconstructing their fields of view individually. The resulting system delivers exceptional sensitivity and wide-area coverage simultaneously, making it ideally suited for alert-based monitoring missions that identify transient high-energy phenomena.

We introduce a new approach to infer the non-linear evolution of the dark matter density spectrum across a wide range of wavenumbers ($k$) by employing deep neural networks trained solely on linear theory predictions. By applying this method to simulations incorporating the speed gauge framework, we uncover significant non-linear corrections emerging at $k \sim 0.2\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ that are directly tied to speed-field contributions. Leveraging these corrections, we develop a refined model for the non-linear density spectrum valid up to $k \sim 0.4\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ in standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. Subsequently, we utilize this enhanced spectral model to boost predictions for the dark matter halo mass function (HMFL) in $\Lambda$CDS, achieving accuracy with a maximum relative error of approximately 10% at $k \sim 0.6\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ in $\Lambda$CDS. Notably, our speed-based model consistently outperforms conventional non-perturbative methods, such as effective field theory of large-scale structure (EFT-LSS), particularly at higher $k$ values where it achieves roughly half the error rate. Precise metrology of local magnetic field fluctuations is crucial for fundamental physics experiments, such as those testing the equivalence principle, which rely on ultra-sensitive atomic sensors like atom interferometers. However, these high-precision instruments are exceptionally susceptible to extrinsic magnetic noise, a problem that becomes particularly acute in the context of atomic clock-based tests of local Lorentz invariance involving spin-precession. Addressing this challenge, we introduce a compact, passive magnetic shield designed specifically for atom interferometric setups. This shield utilizes the Meier effect exhibited by superconductors to deflect stray magnetic fields. We report experimental results demonstrating the detection of local magnetic field variations as small as 100 nT via atomic interferometry using this technique. These measurements were conducted by monitoring the phase shift in an atom interferometer as a cold, superconducting lead was moved through the sensitive region of the sensor. The observed sensitivity to mechanical motion of the shield corresponds to a resolution of approximately 10 pT/√Hz at 1 Hz. Furthermore, the system's ability to detect these minute fields is contingent upon the presence of an image current within the superconductor, a phenomenon we verified by showing that the signal vanishes when the image current is suppressed.

We report a fully relativistic first-principles investigation of the intrinsic characteristics of Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states generated by magnetic impurities. Utilizing the generalized eigenvalue formulation within a tight-binding framework, we derive an effective two-band Hamiltonian for a surface system comprising a single occupied Nb(110) surface $d$-orbital and a single spin $z$-component of an adsorbed $d$-orbital from an impurity. By fitting parameters derived from bulk and surface calculations, we qualitatively reproduce the experimentally observed superconducting gap narrowing in Nb(110) monolayers deposited on Nb(110) single crystals. Furthermore, we predict the spectral signatures resulting from local magnetic moments suppressed by proximity effects. Specifically, we examine how an Mn adatom and various Mn ad clusters on a Nb(110) single crystal exhibit bound states within the superconducting gap. These findings align with recent atomic-resolution scanning tunneling spectroscopy results, which reveal the presence of Molecule-like YSR states for Mn ad clusters on a Nb(110) single crystal.

Skin cancer represents a severe global health challenge, with early detection being critical for effective treatment. Traditional diagnostic methods rely heavily on the specialized expertise of dermatologists, yet these approaches face constraints regarding efficiency and the difficulty of managing large datasets. Consequently, there is a pressing need for automated systems capable of delivering rapid, accurate diagnoses. Additionally, the presence of outlier samples—uncommon cases with distinct characteristics—can significantly hinder the performance of deep learning models trained on standard datasets. This study introduces an innovative deep learning architecture designed to simultaneously resolve the issues of large-scale data processing and the misclassification of outliers. The proposed framework employs a two-stage process: first, a novel Entropy-based Outlier Detection (EOD) method identifies anomalous samples within the dataset; second, a specialized deep neural network, termed the Skin Cancer Diagnostic Network (SCDN), utilizes these identified outliers for enhanced training. Evaluation results using the ISIC 2018 dataset demonstrate the superiority of this approach, achieving a 98.73% accuracy rate for general skin lesion diagnosis and a 97.5% reduction in error rates when specifically handling outlier cases compared to existing methods.

This new system, which we call $\mathcal{Y}$, is conservative over classical first-order Peano arithmetic and uniquely integrates the concepts of validity and truth into its logical structure. The theory $\mathcal{Y}$ serves to axiomatize elementary arithmetic in an extension that is decidable, distinguishing it from the undecidable nature of its parent system. Furthermore, the validity logic in $\mathcal{Y}$ is characterized as the minimal classical first-order theory that includes the $w$-axioms and the diagonal lemma; notably, this specific validity logic is itself decidable. Building upon these foundations, we define an extension of $\mathcal{Y}$ that mirrors the relationship found between second-order Peano arithmetic and its first-order counterpart. We demonstrate the nonexistence of invariant surfaces for specific fractional order dynamical systems, a property that extends the validity of Liouville's theorem for fractional dynamics. Furthermore, we establish the nonexistence of such invariant sets for fractional order systems in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that are locally conjugated to a linear form in the neighborhood of fixed points. These findings indicate that the linear Liouville theorem for fractional dynamics serves as a crucial element in proving the nonexistence of invariant surfaces.

This study examines an inverse problem involving an air-filled rectangular pipe containing a partially submerged elastic plate, which is exposed to an acoustic environment on its upper side. The governing equations consist of coupled hyperbolic and elliptic partial differential equations, solved using a Fourier spectral method in the longitudinal direction and a finite difference approach for the transverse dimension. The solution to the resulting discrete system is advanced in time via a fully implicit scheme. The primary objective is to reconstruct specific initial conditions of the plate from the acoustic velocity potential at the computational domain's boundary, where these conditions are subject to Dirichlet constraints. The reconstruction of the initial data relies on solving a Cauchy problem at the domain limit, complemented by a logarithmically stable, iterative regularization technique designed for the ill-conditioned nature of the inverse mapping. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology. For detailed information regarding the initial conditions of the plate, please consult the original source: A. Buhain, A. Kharchevsky, and A. Yefremov, "Inverse problem of acoustic-structural interaction with logarithmically stable, iterative regularization," *Journal of Computational Mathematics*, 2020, Vol. 28, No. 4, pp. 333–348.

We examine the phenomenology of the minimal scoto-seesaw framework, the most elementary extension of the basic Scoto model capable of realizing neutrino mass generation via the seesaw mechanism. Although the minimal scoto-seaw model introduces two additional Higgs singlets relative to the simplest One-SEeSaw variant, it remains more parsimonious than both the canonical Type-I and Type-II neutrino seesaw models. Within the minimal scoto-seaw framework, we establish the tree-level relationships connecting the parameters of the Standard Model to those of the complete theory, detailing a numerical approach for solving these constraints, and investigating the phenomenology of dark matter in the minimal scoto-seaw framework. We demonstrate that the minimal scoto-seaw model offers a compelling explanation for dark matter, with the candidate being a stable neutral scalar particle from the extended sector. We analyze the dark matter relic density, the LHC production cross-sections for dark matter and associated signatures at the Large Hadron Collider, and direct search constraints from the ATLAS and CMS experiments. We also examine dark matter detection prospects at the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, Higgs vacuum stability, and the radiative corrections to the masses of new scalars in the minimal scoto-seaw framework.
